title: AI Turns a Routine ECG Into a Powerful Predictor of Hidden Heart Artery Disease
source_used: Scienmag (text read on the Bioengineer.org copy)
key_facts: A prospective study in PLOS Digital Health, led by Salah Al-Zaiti, tested the ECG-SMART AI score on symptomatic outpatients scheduled for elective coronary angiography at one tertiary medical centre.
The model was originally trained to spot acute coronary occlusion (a completely blocked heart artery during a heart attack).
The study enrolled 363 patients (average age about 59); each had a standard 12-lead ECG analysed offline by the model.
36.1 percent had angiographically significant disease (at least 70 percent narrowing in a major vessel or 50 percent in the left main artery).
The score put 44 percent of patients at intermediate-to-high risk and 56 percent at low risk; the higher-risk group had an odds ratio of 3.12 after adjusting for clinical characteristics.
AUROC was 0.79 (95 percent CI 0.74 to 0.84), with 60 percent precision at 80 percent recall.

It was a single-centre study in a population already selected for angiography, so results will shift in lower-prevalence settings; the authors say the score complements, not replaces, clinical judgment.
quote_evidence: The study enrolled 363 patients, with an average age of about 59 years and a slight male majority.
Overall, 36.1 percent of the patients had angiographically significant disease.

The study was conducted at a single tertiary center in a population already selected for elective angiography, so the prevalence of significant disease, 36 percent, is far higher than in the general population of symptomatic outpatients.
why_it_matters_hint: A cheap ECG plus AI might help decide who needs an invasive heart procedure, but it is one-centre evidence in a pre-selected group.
event_date: Scienmag article dated 10 Oct 2026; study publication date not stated
